# CLAUDE.md

Project memory for Claude Code. Loaded automatically at the start of every session.

## What this project is

A take-home assessment for Nuuly: a small inventory REST API (receive stock by SKU,
process purchases, report inventory levels). Full brief: [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).

**It is also a Kotlin master class.** Robert is learning Kotlin and wants to use this
project to learn it properly, whatever happens with the interview. Every piece of
code must teach as well as work. Treat "can Robert explain every line of this in the
follow-up interview?" as a requirement alongside passing the tests.

## Source of truth

- **API contract:** [docs/open_api/inventory.yaml](docs/open_api/inventory.yaml). Paths, status codes,
  content types and schemas must match it exactly. Error responses (400/404) are
  `text/plain` strings, not JSON. `quantity` in requests has `minimum: 1`.
- If the contract is ambiguous (e.g. malformed JSON, missing body, SKU id format),
  stop and ask Robert rather than guessing; record the decision in the README.

## Task list

[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md) is the working task list. Read it at the start of each session,
check items off as they are done, and add new items as they come up. Its **oversell protection
test plan** is a hard requirement: a purchase must never oversell, even under concurrent requests.
Every feature that touches stock must add or extend tests from that plan.

## Stack

- Kotlin on the JVM, Spring Boot (Spring MVC), Gradle with the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`).
  Chosen because it is what Nuuly runs in production.
- PostgreSQL (run with Docker Compose; Testcontainers in tests). Stock changes are single atomic
  SQL statements, backed by `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`. See the README decision record.
- Tests: JUnit 5 with Spring's test support.
- Open decisions are tracked in the README under "Open decisions". Do not settle
  one silently; propose it, explain the trade-offs, and let Robert choose.

## Commenting and documentation standard (teaching mode)

This goes further than normal production code on purpose. Follow it for every `.kt` file.

1. **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: classes, interfaces, objects, and functions.
   Say what it does, why it exists, and where it sits in the request flow
   (controller → service → repository). Use `@param`, `@return`, and `@throws` when
   they add information. Test classes get a KDoc saying what they cover.
   A PostToolUse hook ([scripts/check_kdoc.py](scripts/check_kdoc.py)) enforces this mechanically.
2. **Tagged inline comments** explain the concepts, not the syntax. Use these prefixes so
   they can be searched (`grep -rn "// Kotlin:" src`):
   - `// Kotlin:` a Kotlin language feature (data class, null safety, `val` vs `var`,
     scope functions, extension functions, `when`, default arguments, sealed types...).
     Add a note on how Java would do it when that helps.
   - `// Spring:` framework behavior that is otherwise invisible: what an annotation
     does, how dependency injection wires this, what auto-configuration provides,
     how a request is mapped or a response is serialized.
   - `// Why:` a design decision and the alternative that was rejected.
   - `// Contract:` the line exists to satisfy a specific part of inventory.yaml.
3. Explain a concept in full the first time it appears in a file. After that, a short
   tag is enough. Longer explanations go in [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
4. Do not narrate trivial statements (`// increment counter`). Every comment should
   teach something or record a decision.
5. `build.gradle.kts` and `application.yml` get the same treatment: comment each plugin,
   dependency and setting with what it is for.

## Feature workflow

Use `/feature <description>` for any new behavior. It runs the whole loop:
contract check → plan (Robert approves) → tests + implementation → build →
`doc-reviewer` agent → README update → hand-off to `/walkthrough`.

- **Do not start the next feature until the walkthrough for the current one is done.**
- After the walkthrough, fix any comment that turned out to be unclear.
- Keep changes small and commit-sized. The reviewers want a readable, unsquashed
  git history. Propose a commit message, but only commit when Robert says so or runs `/ship`.

## Git workflow: never work on main

- **Every session starts on a new branch.** If the session starts on `main`, ask Robert what the
  session's work is before touching anything, then run
  `git switch main && git pull --ff-only && git switch -c <type>/<slug>`, where `<type>` is
  `feature`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs` or `test` (e.g. `feature/get-inventory`).
- One branch per piece of work. Commit in small, logical steps; the reviewers read the history.
- **`/ship`** is the only way work reaches `main`: push → PR → merge commit → back to an
  updated `main`. Never squash or rebase merges (the brief says "Do not squash commits").
- Enforced by `scripts/branch_guard.py`:
  - a `SessionStart` hook flags when the session starts on `main`
  - a `PreToolUse` hook blocks, while on `main`, edits to repo files and `git commit`/`git push`
  - on any branch, it blocks pushes to `main` and squash/rebase merges

## Project tooling (.claude/)

- `skills/feature/`: the `/feature` workflow above.
- `skills/walkthrough/`: `/walkthrough`, an interactive line-by-line teaching session
  on recent changes, logged to [docs/learning/walkthroughs/](docs/learning/walkthroughs/).
- `skills/ship/`: `/ship`, which pushes the current branch, opens a PR, and merges it into
  `main` with a merge commit. Build, test and review gates will be added later.
- `agents/doc-reviewer.md`: read-only reviewer that checks changed code against the
  commenting standard above.
- `TODO.md`: the working task list.
- `settings.json` hooks:
  - `SessionStart` + `PreToolUse`: `scripts/branch_guard.py` (see Git workflow).
  - `Stop`: exports session transcripts to [docs/ai-sessions/](docs/ai-sessions/).
  - `PostToolUse` (Edit/Write): runs `scripts/check_kdoc.py` on edited `.kt` files and
    reports missing KDoc back to Claude.

## Environment

Windows 11. Claude has PowerShell and Git Bash available. Python is on PATH and is
used for the hook scripts.

===== docs/learning/notes/build.gradle.kts.md
     1	# build.gradle.kts
     2	
     3	> Source: [build.gradle.kts](../../../build.gradle.kts) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23
     4	
     5	## Role
     6	
     7	The build definition: which compiler and plugins to use, which libraries the app and tests
     8	depend on, and how tests run. Generated by Spring Initializr (the command is in the commit
     9	"Generate the Spring Boot project with Spring Initializr") and then trimmed.
    10	
    11	## Walkthrough
    12	
    13	### The file is Kotlin: trailing lambdas
    14	
    15	```kotlin
    16	plugins {
    17	    ...
    18	}
    19	```
    20	
    21	**Kotlin:** `plugins { ... }` is a *function call*. Its only argument is a lambda, and Kotlin
    22	lets a lambda that is the last argument move outside the parentheses. When it's the only
    23	argument, the parentheses disappear entirely. So `plugins { }` is really `plugins({ })`.
    24	Inside the lambda, `this` is a Gradle object (a "lambda with receiver"), which is why you can
    25	call `id(...)` or `kotlin(...)` without a prefix. This pattern is called a **type-safe builder**,
    26	and it's how Kotlin DSLs (Gradle, Ktor, kotlinx.html) read like configuration.
    27	
    28	### Plugins
    29	
    30	```kotlin
    31	kotlin("jvm") version "2.3.21"
    32	// Opens Spring-annotated classes: Kotlin classes are final by default, Spring needs to subclass some.
    33	kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.3.21"
    34	id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.1"
    35	// Supplies versions from Spring Boot's BOM, so most dependencies below have none.
    36	id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
    37	```
    38	
    39	**Kotlin:** `kotlin("jvm")` is shorthand for `id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm")`. `version` is an
    40	**infix function**: `a version b` means `a.version(b)`. Any single-argument function marked
    41	`infix` can be called that way.
    42	
    43	- **`kotlin("jvm")`**: runs the Kotlin compiler and targets the JVM.
    44	- **`kotlin("plugin.spring")`**: Kotlin classes and functions are **final by default** (Java is
    45	  the opposite; you have to write `final`). Spring sometimes creates a runtime *subclass* of
    46	  your bean (a proxy) to add behavior, e.g. `@Transactional` or `@Configuration`, and it can't
    47	  subclass a final class. This compiler plugin ("all-open") automatically makes classes with
    48	  Spring annotations `open`, so we don't have to write `open` everywhere.
    49	- **`org.springframework.boot`**: adds `bootRun` (run from source) and `bootJar` (one runnable
    50	  "fat" jar that contains all dependencies).
    51	- **`io.spring.dependency-management`**: imports Spring Boot's **BOM** (bill of materials), a
    52	  list of library versions tested together.
    53	
    54	**Why:** we have no version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`). The BOM already pins nearly every
    55	version, so a catalog would add indirection for no benefit.
    56	
    57	### Group, version and the Java toolchain
    58	
    59	```kotlin
    60	group = "com.robertwoolbright"
    61	version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"
    62	
    63	java {
    64	    toolchain {
    65	        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    66	    }
    67	}
    68	```
    69	
    70	**Kotlin:** `languageVersion = ...` looks like a field assignment. Gradle properties are lazy
    71	`Property<T>` objects, though, and Gradle's Kotlin DSL turns `=` into a call to `.set(...)`.
    72	Older builds write `languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(21))`.
    73	
    74	**Why:** a toolchain makes Gradle compile and test with JDK 21, whichever JDK is running Gradle
    75	itself (Gradle finds or downloads one). Anyone who clones the repo builds with the same Java
    76	version. The Kotlin plugin reads the toolchain too, so the bytecode targets Java 21.
    77	
    78	### Dependencies: configurations
    79	
    80	```kotlin
    81	dependencies {
    82	    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-flyway")
    83	    ...
    84	    developmentOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-docker-compose")
    85	    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
    86	    testImplementation(...)
    87	    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
    88	}
    89	```
    90	
    91	The function name in front of each dependency (its *configuration*) decides where it's visible:
    92	
    93	| Configuration | Visible to |
    94	| --- | --- |
    95	| `implementation` | app code at compile time and at runtime |
    96	| `runtimeOnly` | runtime only; our code never refers to it by name |
    97	| `developmentOnly` | `bootRun` only; left out of tests and of the jar |
    98	| `testImplementation` / `testRuntimeOnly` | the same idea, for `src/test` |
    99	
   100	**Spring:** a **starter** is a dependency that brings a coherent set of libraries plus the
   101	auto-configuration for them. Spring Boot 4 split the starters into smaller modules, which is why
   102	Flyway, JDBC and Web MVC each have their own starter and test starter.
   103	
   104	### App dependencies
   105	
   106	| Dependency | What it gives us |
   107	| --- | --- |
   108	| `spring-boot-starter-flyway` | Runs the SQL migrations in `src/main/resources/db/migration` at startup, before any request is served. |
   109	| `flyway-database-postgresql` | Since Flyway 10, support for most databases, Postgres included, is a separate module. Without it, Flyway refuses to talk to Postgres. |
   110	| `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` | A pooled `DataSource` (HikariCP), `JdbcClient`/`JdbcTemplate` and a transaction manager, all auto-configured. `JdbcClient` is our data-access API. |
   111	| `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` | Spring MVC on an embedded Tomcat, plus Jackson for JSON. (Boot 4 introduced `starter-webmvc`; the old `starter-web` still exists but is deprecated.) |
   112	| `kotlin-reflect` | Lets Spring read Kotlin metadata that Java reflection can't see, such as whether a parameter is nullable and whether it has a default value. |
   113	| `jackson-module-kotlin` | Teaches Jackson to build Kotlin classes. A `data class` with `val` properties has no no-arg constructor and no setters; this module calls the primary constructor and respects non-null types and default values. `tools.jackson` is **Jackson 3**'s group ID (Boot 4 moved to Jackson 3). |
   114	| `spring-boot-docker-compose` | On `bootRun`, runs `docker compose up` on `compose.yaml` and points the DataSource at it. See [compose.yaml notes](compose.yaml.md). |
   115	| `postgresql` | The JDBC driver. We code only against the standard `java.sql` interfaces, so it's `runtimeOnly`. |
   116	
   117	### Test dependencies
   118	
   119	| Dependency | What it gives us |
   120	| --- | --- |
   121	| `spring-boot-starter-{flyway,jdbc,webmvc}-test` | Test support for each module, e.g. `@WebMvcTest` + `MockMvc` and `@JdbcTest`. They also pull in `spring-boot-starter-test`: JUnit Jupiter 6, AssertJ, Mockito. |
   122	| `spring-boot-testcontainers` | `@ServiceConnection`, which turns a running container into DataSource settings. |
   123	| `kotlin-test-junit5` | `kotlin.test` assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertFailsWith`) backed by JUnit Jupiter. The artifact keeps its old `junit5` name, but it runs fine on JUnit 6. |
   124	| `testcontainers-junit-jupiter`, `testcontainers-postgresql` | Start a real Postgres in Docker for tests. |
   125	| `junit-platform-launcher` | Gradle 9 no longer bundles the JUnit Platform launcher; it has to be on the test runtime classpath. |
   126	
   127	**Why:** tests run against real Postgres instead of H2, an in-memory database that imitates
   128	others. Our oversell protection depends on Postgres-specific behavior (`ON CONFLICT`, row locks
   129	during `UPDATE`, `CHECK` constraints), and H2 imitates those imperfectly.

   131	### Compiler options
   132	
   133	```kotlin
   134	kotlin {
   135	    compilerOptions {
   136	        freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xjsr305=strict", "-Xannotation-default-target=param-property")
   137	    }
   138	}
   139	```
   140	
   141	**Kotlin:** Kotlin's null safety (`String` can never be null; `String?` can) stops at the edge of
   142	Java code, because Java types carry no nullability. Kotlin treats an unannotated Java type as a
   143	**platform type**, shown as `String!`: you may treat it as nullable or not, and if you guess
   144	wrong you get a runtime NPE. Many Java libraries annotate their APIs instead.
   145	- **`-Xjsr305=strict`**: turns the JSR-305 annotations (`@Nonnull` / `@Nullable`) into real
   146	  `String` / `String?` types, so a mistake becomes a compile error. Spring Framework 7 uses the
   147	  newer JSpecify annotations, which Kotlin 2 already enforces; this flag covers libraries still
   148	  on JSR-305.
   149	- **`-Xannotation-default-target=param-property`**: in `class Q(@Ann val x: Int)`, the one
   150	  `val x` is a constructor parameter, a property and a backing field all at once, so an
   151	  annotation on it is ambiguous. This option puts it on the parameter, **and** on the property
   152	  if the annotation is allowed to target a property; otherwise on the backing field. Java
   153	  annotations such as `@NotBlank` or `@JsonProperty` can't target a Kotlin property, so they land
   154	  on the parameter and the field. Those are the places Bean Validation and Jackson look.
   155	  This will become Kotlin's default in a future release.
   156	
   157	### Tests run on the JUnit Platform
   158	
   159	```kotlin
   160	tasks.withType<Test> {
   161	    useJUnitPlatform()
   162	}
   163	```
   164	
   165	Spring Boot 4 manages **JUnit 6**. The test API we write against (`org.junit.jupiter.api.Test`)
   166	is the same Jupiter API as JUnit 5. `useJUnitPlatform()` tells Gradle to run tests through the
   167	JUnit Platform rather than the legacy JUnit 4 runner.
   168	
   169	**Kotlin:** `withType<Test>` uses a **reified type parameter**. On the JVM, generic types are
   170	normally erased at runtime, but an `inline` function can mark its type parameter `reified` and
   171	use it as a real class. So you write `withType<Test>` instead of Java's
   172	`withType(Test.class)`. The trailing lambda then configures every `Test` task.

     4	
     5	## Role
     6	
     7	Defines the Postgres container used when you run the app locally with `./gradlew bootRun`.
     8	Tests don't use it; they use Testcontainers (see
     9	[TestcontainersConfiguration notes](test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).
    10	
    11	## Walkthrough
    12	
    13	### Who runs this file
    14	
    15	```yaml
    16	# Local Postgres for `./gradlew bootRun`. Spring Boot's Docker Compose support starts and stops
    17	# it automatically. Tests don't use this file; they use Testcontainers.
    18	```
    19	
    20	**Spring:** you never run `docker compose up` yourself. The `spring-boot-docker-compose`
    21	dependency (`developmentOnly` in the build) finds `compose.yaml` at startup, starts it, and waits
    22	until the container is running and its mapped port accepts TCP connections. (That's Spring's
    23	default readiness check. It would use a compose `healthcheck` if we defined one.) It then reads the container's image, environment and mapped port
    24	and builds the DataSource connection details from them (a JDBC URL, user and password). On
    25	shutdown it stops the container. You can see this in the `bootRun` log: `Container ... Started`,
    26	then Flyway connecting to `jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:<port>/inventory`.
    27	
    28	### Image version
    29	
    30	```yaml
    31	image: 'postgres:18'
    32	```
    33	
    34	**Why:** pinned to a major version instead of `latest`, so a new Postgres major release can't
    35	change behavior without us noticing. `18` still receives the 18.x patch releases. Tests
    36	use the same tag, so local runs and tests behave the same.
    37	
    38	### Credentials
    39	
    40	```yaml
    41	environment:
    42	  - 'POSTGRES_DB=inventory'
    43	  - 'POSTGRES_USER=inventory'
    44	  - 'POSTGRES_PASSWORD=inventory'
    45	```
    46	
    47	The official Postgres image creates this database and user on first start. These are throwaway,
    48	local-only values. Spring reads them from here, so they aren't repeated in `application.yml`.
    49	
    50	### Ports
    51	
    52	```yaml
    53	ports:
    54	  # Why: random free host port (no clash with a local Postgres), bound to 127.0.0.1 only so the
    55	  # dev database isn't reachable from the network. Plain '5432' would bind on all interfaces.
    56	  - '127.0.0.1::5432'
    57	```
    58	
    59	The format is `host-ip:host-port:container-port`, and here the host port is left empty.
    60	
    61	**Why:** the host port is empty, so Docker picks a random free one (e.g. `53106`). A fixed
    62	`'5432:5432'` would fail if you already had Postgres running locally. Spring asks Docker which
    63	port it got, so nothing needs to know the number in advance.
    64	
    65	**Why `127.0.0.1`:** by default Docker publishes ports on *all* network interfaces. Other
    66	machines on your Wi-Fi could then reach a database whose password is `inventory`. Binding to
    67	the loopback address keeps it on this machine.

     2	
     3	> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplication.kt](../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/InventoryApplication.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-23
     4	
     5	## Role
     6	
     7	The entry point. `./gradlew bootRun` (or `java -jar`) calls `main`, which starts Spring. Spring
     8	then finds every controller, service and repository and wires them together. No request ever
     9	passes through this file, but none could be served without it.
    10	
    11	## Walkthrough
    12	
    13	### The package
    14	
    15	```kotlin
    16	package com.robertwoolbright.inventory
    17	```
    18	
    19	**Kotlin:** same as Java, except the directory doesn't *have* to match the package in Kotlin. We
    20	keep them matching anyway because that's the convention and Spring's scan relies on packages.
    21	
    22	**Why:** this file sits in the *root* package on purpose. See `@ComponentScan` below.
    23	
    24	### `@SpringBootApplication` and a class with no body
    25	
    26	```kotlin
    27	@SpringBootApplication
    28	class InventoryApplication
    29	```
    30	
    31	**Spring:** `@SpringBootApplication` combines three annotations:
    32	
    33	| Annotation | Effect |
    34	| --- | --- |
    35	| `@SpringBootConfiguration` | A specialized `@Configuration`: this class may declare `@Bean` methods, and it's what `@SpringBootTest` searches for. |
    36	| `@EnableAutoConfiguration` | Configure whatever the classpath implies: Tomcat because Web MVC is present, a `DataSource` because JDBC + the Postgres driver are, Flyway, Jackson… |
    37	| `@ComponentScan` | Find `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository` and `@RestController` classes **in this package and its sub-packages**, and create them as beans. |
    38	
    39	That scan is why the file lives at `com.robertwoolbright.inventory`: the future
    40	`inventory.InventoryController` sits below it and gets found automatically.
    41	
    42	**Kotlin:** a class with no body needs no `{}`. Spring never calls anything on this class; it
    43	only reads the annotations. It must still be a `class` rather than an `object` (Kotlin's
    44	singleton), because Spring wants to create and proxy configuration classes itself. The
    45	`plugin.spring` compiler plugin makes it `open` so Spring can subclass it. See the
    46	[build notes](../build.gradle.kts.md).
    47	
    48	### Top-level `main`
    49	
    50	```kotlin
    51	/** Starts Spring: builds the application context, runs Flyway migrations and starts Tomcat. */
    52	fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    53	    runApplication<InventoryApplication>(*args)
    54	}
    55	```
    56	
    57	**Kotlin: top-level functions.** `main` isn't inside any class. Kotlin allows functions at file
    58	level. The compiler still has to put bytecode in a class, so it generates one named after the
    59	file: `InventoryApplicationKt`, with a `public static void main(String[] args)`. The startup log
    60	shows it: `Started InventoryApplicationKt in 5.9 seconds`. In Java, `main` must be a static
    61	method written inside a class.
    62	
    63	**Kotlin: `Array<String>`** is Java's `String[]`. Kotlin arrays are an ordinary generic class, not
    64	special syntax.
    65	
    66	**Kotlin: reified generics.** `runApplication<InventoryApplication>(...)` names the class in angle
    67	brackets. It's an `inline` function with a `reified` type parameter, so it can use `T::class` at
    68	runtime (normally generics are erased). The Java equivalent:
    69	`SpringApplication.run(InventoryApplication.class, args)`.
    70	
    71	**Kotlin: spread operator.** `runApplication` takes `vararg args: String`, so inside the
    72	function `args` is an `Array<String>`, but *callers* must pass individual `String`s. Passing
    73	`args` without the `*` doesn't compile: an `Array<String>` isn't a `String`. `*args` spreads the
    74	array's elements into the vararg. (Java accepts an array where a vararg is expected; Kotlin makes
    75	you say so. You can also mix: `runApplication<X>("--debug", *args)`.)
    76	
    77	**Spring:** `runApplication` creates the application context. It runs auto-configuration,
    78	creates every bean (including the Flyway bean, which applies migrations while starting up),
    79	starts Tomcat on port 8080, and then returns. The JVM stays alive because Tomcat's threads
    80	are still running.
    81

    85	- What is the name of the JVM class that contains `main`, and why?
    86	- Why doesn't `runApplication<InventoryApplication>(args)` (no `*`) compile?

     4	
     5	## Role
     6	
     7	Shared test setup. Any test that imports it gets a real Postgres 18 running in Docker, with the
     8	app's DataSource pointed at it. Every repository, controller and concurrency test builds on this.
     9	
    10	## Walkthrough
    11	
    12	### `@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)`
    13	
    14	```kotlin
    15	@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    16	class TestcontainersConfiguration {
    17	```
    18	
    19	**Spring:** `@TestConfiguration` is a `@Configuration` meant only for tests. Component scanning
    20	from `@SpringBootApplication` deliberately skips it, so the container exists only in tests that
    21	ask for it with `@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)`.
    22	
    23	**Spring: `proxyBeanMethods`.** By default Spring subclasses a `@Configuration` class so that
    24	when one `@Bean` method calls another, you get the existing bean instead of a new object. We have
    25	one bean and no such calls, so turning the proxy off is faster and changes nothing.
    26	
    27	**Kotlin: named arguments.** `proxyBeanMethods = false` names the parameter it sets. Named
    28	arguments work when calling Kotlin functions and for annotation parameters, but **not** for Java
    29	methods, whose parameter names Kotlin can't rely on. For a Java annotation like this one,
    30	every parameter except `value` *must* be named. `@TestConfiguration(false)` wouldn't compile,
    31	because a positional argument goes to `value` (a `String`).
    32	
    33	### The container bean
    34	
    35	```kotlin
    36	@Bean
    37	@ServiceConnection
    38	fun postgresContainer(): PostgreSQLContainer =
    39	    // Why: same major version as compose.yaml, so tests and local runs behave the same.
    40	    PostgreSQLContainer(DockerImageName.parse("postgres:18"))
    41	```
    42	
    43	**Spring: `@Bean`.** The return value becomes a Spring-managed object. Testcontainers containers
    44	are `Startable`, and Spring Boot starts them when the bean is created and stops them when the
    45	context closes.
    46	
    47	**Spring: `@ServiceConnection`.** This annotation is what connects the container to the app. Spring Boot sees a
    48	`PostgreSQLContainer`, asks it for its JDBC URL, username and password (random host port, test
    49	credentials), and registers them as the connection details. Those override any
    50	`spring.datasource.*` setting.
    51	
    52	**Spring: context caching.** Spring caches test application contexts and reuses one for any
    53	test class whose *whole* configuration is identical, so those classes share one container.
    54	A different setup (a slice like `@WebMvcTest` or `@JdbcTest`, extra properties, a
    55	`@MockitoBean`) gets its own context and its own container. Cached contexts stay alive until
    56	the test JVM exits, so several Postgres containers can be running at once.
    57	
    58	**Kotlin: expression body.** `fun f(): T = expr` replaces `fun f(): T { return expr }` when the
    59	body is a single expression. The return type could be inferred, but we keep it because it's
    60	part of what this function promises.
    61	
    62	**Why:** a real Postgres rather than H2. See the [build notes](../../build.gradle.kts.md).
